summary: South Carolina does not regulate keeping pet rodents. Its only exotic-pet ban (Title 47, ch. 2) reaches just large wild cats, non-native bears, and great apes; its carnivore-sale ban (§47-5-50) doesn't touch rodents; and the wildlife-import chapter expressly EXEMPTS 'rats and mice' imported for the pet trade from any permit (§50-16-60). So keeping, breeding, and selling/giving a captive-bred roof rat is effectively legal and unregulated. Two soft points: the universal no-release rule, and confirming with Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health whether any health certificate applies to interstate pet-rodent transport. The one genuine open question is whether the generic phrase 'rats and mice' is read to include the R. rattus species specifically.

keep.why: South Carolina has no permit requirement to keep a pet rodent. The only categorical exotic-pet ban (SC Code §47-2-10 / §47-2-30) reaches only large wild cats, non-native bears, and great apes, rodents are not within it. SCDNR's restricted-non-native list (Reg. 123-152) is tegu-centric and does not list rats. Gemini DR-verified: R. rattus is an unprotected commensal rodent; no captive-wildlife permit is required for non-native rodents kept as pets (SC Code 50-16-10/-60).
keep.governing_law: SC Code §47-2-10 & §47-2-30 (limited exotic ban); SC Code Title 50 ch. 16 & SC Regs. 123-152 (DNR scope; rats not listed).

breed.why: No South Carolina law licenses or restricts breeding pet rodents, the breeder statutes cover dogs (and registrable companion dogs/cats) only. DNR's pet-import exemption for 'rats and mice' (§50-16-60) signals the pet-trade is unregulated. Breeding is unregulated rather than expressly permitted. Gemini DR-verified: no state breeder/facility license for small mammals.
breed.governing_law: SC Code §47-3-1010 et seq. & §47-13-160 (breeder scope = dogs/cats); SC Code §50-16-60.

sell_give.why: The wild-carnivore-sale ban (§47-5-50) doesn't reach rodents, and the pet-sale disclosure law applies only to dogs/cats. DNR's importation chapter expressly exempts 'rats and mice … imported for sale as pets' from the permit requirement (§50-16-60). No state license is needed to sell or give pet rats, though local business-license rules may apply. Gemini DR-verified: 50-16-60 exempts 'rats and mice' for the pet trade; no state pet-shop/dealer license.
sell_give.governing_law: SC Code §47-5-50 (carnivore-sale ban, inapplicable); §47-13-160 (dogs/cats); §50-16-60 (rats/mice pet exemption).

transport.why: For wildlife-import purposes, §50-16-60 places 'rats and mice' on the no-DNR-permit list, and the §50-16-20 import-permit species list excludes rodents. Animal-health import is run by Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health; its CVI/rabies rules center on livestock/poultry/dogs/cats/ferrets, with no published rule imposing a CVI on pet rats, but confirm before interstate movement. Never release a non-native rat. Gemini DR-verified: Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health requires a 30-day CVI for wildlife/exotics entering SC, even though SCDNR waives the wildlife import permit for 'rats and mice'; within-state movement unregulated.
transport.governing_law: SC Code §50-16-20 & §50-16-60 (import-permit list excludes rodents; pet rat/mouse exemption); SC Regs. ch. 27 (Clemson LPH import rules).

restrictions.summary: Never release or let escape a roof rat, Title 50 ch. 16 prohibits releasing imported wildlife, and R. rattus is itself an established invasive. Rehome responsibly.

inquiry_focus: (1) Does the §50-16-60 pet-trade exemption for 'rats and mice' include Rattus rattus (the roof/black rat, distinct from the common fancy rat Rattus norvegicus), or does SCDNR consider R. rattus a regulated non-native species requiring an import/possession permit under §50-16-20 or Reg. 123-152? (2) For interstate transport of pet rats into or out of South Carolina, does Clemson Livestock-Poultry Health require a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection or any health-entry permit for pet rodents?
